summary: An informational framework outlining the issues in providing IP Integrated Services with RSVP over ATM.

plainLanguage.summary: RSVP lets a receiver ask for a reserved quality of service on a connection, and ATM lets a network set up a circuit with a promised quality. RFC 2382 works out how the two fit together: what the service model maps onto, which circuit carries which traffic, and how the messages that set it all up travel.

questions: integrated services and rsvp over atm
how do rsvp and atm work together
how to manage atm virtual circuits for rsvp
what is multicast heterogeneity in rsvp over atm
what is the rsvp over atm framework
subtitle: How the Internet's reservation protocol was meant to work over ATM's virtual circuits

tldr.problem: The Internet offered one class of service, best effort, and real-time traffic such as voice and video worked well only across unloaded parts of the network. RSVP and the Integrated Services model were being introduced to fix that, and ATM underneath could reserve a circuit with a stated quality of service, but the two did not fit together.
tldr.mechanism: The memo frames the problem as two questions: how to map the Integrated Services service models onto ATM service categories and traffic parameters, and how to manage the ATM virtual circuits that carry both the reserved traffic and the RSVP messages that set it up.
tldr.outcome: It is a framework rather than a specification. It sets out the modes and models, four ways of handling receivers that ask for different service, several ways of giving the control messages a path of their own, and the encapsulation rules that follow.

facts.value: At most two: one best effort and one with quality of service

facts.label: Signalling circuits in the network core
facts.value: Approximately n(n-1)/2 where n is the number of IP nodes

today: RFC 2382 is an Informational memo that has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a framework document written to frame the problems for the follow-on papers in the same working group, which cover the service model mapping and the implementation requirements and guidelines.

sections.title: Why RSVP over ATM Is Not Straightforward
sections.content:
The Internet had one class of service, best effort, typified by first-come, first-serve scheduling at each hop. It worked well for electronic mail, web access and file transfer, but for real-time traffic such as voice and video the Internet performed well only across unloaded portions of the network. New classes of service and a quality of service signalling protocol were being introduced, and that protocol was RSVP, the Resource ReSerVation Protocol, together with the Internet Integrated Services model, while best effort was retained.

One of the important features of ATM is the ability to request a point-to-point virtual circuit with a specified quality of service, and another is the ability to request point-to-multipoint virtual circuits with a specified quality of service. Point-to-multipoint circuits allow leaf nodes to be added and removed dynamically, which provides a mechanism for supporting IP multicast. It is natural, the memo says, for RSVP and Integrated Services to want to use the quality of service properties of any underlying link layer, including ATM, and the memo concentrates on ATM.

Some of the ground had already been covered. Classical IP over ATM solved part of the problem, supporting IP unicast best effort traffic over ATM. It is based on a Logical IP Subnetwork, a separately administered IP subnetwork: hosts within one communicate using the ATM network, while hosts in different subnets communicate only by going through an IP router, even where a direct circuit between them over the ATM network might have been possible. Classical IP over ATM provides an Address Resolution Protocol for ATM edge devices to resolve IP addresses to native ATM addresses, and for any pair of edge devices a single circuit is created on demand and shared for all traffic between them. The other half of the problem, IP multicast, was being solved with MARS, the Multicast Address Resolution Server, which complements ATMARP by allowing an IP address to resolve into a list of native ATM addresses rather than a single one. The ATM Forum's LAN Emulation and Multiprotocol over ATM also address IP best effort traffic over ATM in similar ways.

What remained was the integration of RSVP signalling and ATM signalling in support of the Integrated Services model, and the memo splits that into two areas: QoS translation, which is mapping a service model quality of service onto a proper ATM one, and VC management, which is how many circuits are needed and which traffic flows over which of them. The memo is a guide to these issues, intended to frame the problems that later documents address.
sections.plainLanguage: Two reservation systems with different habits. RSVP asks from the receiver's side and expects the network to sort itself out; ATM sets up a wire with a promised quality from the sender's side. On top of that, IP multicast lets anyone join a group, while ATM needs every receiver named and added to a circuit one at a time. The memo is about reconciling all of that.

sections.title: Modes and Models for Running RSVP over ATM
sections.content:
Any of the IP over ATM models would work as long as the RSVP control packets, which are IP protocol 46, and the data packets can follow the same IP path through the network. It matters that the RSVP PATH messages follow the same IP path as the data, so that the right PATH state can be installed in the routers along the path. For an ATM subnetwork this means the ingress and egress points must be the same in both directions for the control and the data messages. The memo notes that RSVP itself does not require symmetric routing: the PATH state installed by RSVP allows the RESV messages to retrace the hops the PATH message crossed.

Within each IP over ATM model there are decisions about the kind of data distribution to use in ATM and about how connections are initiated. In the User Network Interface 3.0 and 3.1 specifications and the 4.0 specification, both permanent and switched virtual circuits may be established with a specified service category and specific traffic descriptors, in point-to-point and point-to-multipoint configurations. UNI 3.x offers CBR, VBR and UBR, and 4.0 offers VBR-rt and ABR. Additional quality of service parameters are not available in UNI 3.x, and those that are available are vendor-specific, so the level of control in a standard UNI 3.x network is limited, although these building blocks are enough to use RSVP and the service models. ATM 4.0 with the Traffic Management 4.0 specification allows much greater control.

A permanent virtual circuit emulates a dedicated point-to-point line, so the operation of RSVP can be identical to its operation over any point-to-point network. The quality of service of the circuit must be consistent with the traffic and the service model in use, and the devices at either end have to provide traffic control services in order to multiplex several flows over the same circuit. With permanent circuits there is no question of when or how long it takes to set one up, since they are made in advance, but the resources are limited to what was pre-allocated.

The memo also looks forward, at models that would improve the picture: heterogeneous point-to-multipoint circuits, lightweight signalling, quality of service renegotiation, group addressing, and label switching. It also separates the treatment of hop-by-hop operation from the use of short-cuts, where a direct circuit crosses the IP subnetwork boundary.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules that make it work are simple to state: the setup messages and the data must travel the same path, and the two ends must be the same from both directions. On top of that sit choices about which kind of circuit to use, whether it is set up by hand or by signalling, and whether it carries one flow or many.

sections.title: Mapping Service Models and the Loose Ends
sections.content:
Mapping the Integrated Services models onto ATM service categories and quality of service parameters is a matter of deciding which categories can support the goals of a service model and matching the parameters and variables of the service model to those of the ATM description. Because ATM has such a wide variety of service categories and parameters, more than one ATM service category should be able to support each of the two service models, which gives flexibility in configuration and deployment. A separate document examines the Controlled Load and Guaranteed Service models in detail. While guidelines can be drawn for mapping the parameters of a given model onto the traffic descriptors of an ATM traffic class, implementation variables, policy and cost factors can make a strict mapping problematic, so a set of workable mappings that can be applied to different requirements and scenarios is needed, as long as they can satisfy the needs of the model.

Some scaling problems can be addressed by aggregating several RSVP flows over a single circuit when the destinations of the circuit match for all the flows being aggregated. That causes considerable complexity in managing circuits and in scheduling packets within each circuit at the root point of it, and the memo notes that rescheduling flows within a circuit is not possible in the switches in the core of the ATM network. Virtual paths can be used to aggregate multiple circuits.

Hosts directly connected to ATM networks must be considered, and functionality for RSVP over ATM must not assume that an ATM host has all the functionality of a router, though having MARS and NHRP clients would be worthwhile. A host must manage circuits just like any other ATM sender or receiver.

Accounting and policy need study too, because RSVP and Integrated Services create classes of preferential service, so some form of administrative control or cost allocation is needed. Typical IP policies, such as allowing only certain users to make reservations, translate well to IP over ATM because of the similarity to the mechanisms used for call admission control. There may also be policies specific to IP over ATM: since signalling costs in ATM are high relative to IP, a policy might restrict the ability to change the prevailing quality of service in a circuit, and where circuits are scarce there might be specific accounting costs in creating a new one. The memo calls this work preliminary, with much left to do.
sections.plainLanguage: The service models describe quality in the Internet's words; ATM describes it in its own. Someone has to translate, and the translation cannot be rigid, because what a network charges and how it is run also matter. And because a reservation is a privileged thing, somebody has to decide who may make one and what it costs.

sections.title: Managing the Circuits That Carry the Traffic
sections.content:
There is an apparent mismatch between RSVP and ATM: RSVP control is receiver oriented and ATM control is sender oriented. The memo argues this is not as serious as it looks. Although reservation requests are generated at the receiver, the actual allocation of resources takes place at the subnet sender, so subnet senders establish all the quality of service circuits and the subnet receiver must be able to accept incoming ones. These restrictions are consistent with RSVP version 1 processing rules, and they let senders use different flow to circuit mappings, and even different renegotiation techniques, without interoperability problems.

Any implementation must map reserved flows onto ATM circuits. The models that map IP traffic onto ATM circuits, such as Classical IP and NHRP, cover only a single quality of service, that of best effort traffic. When quality of service is introduced, the mapping has to be revisited, because a single point-to-point circuit shared by all traffic between two hosts is unlikely to be adequate or optimal for flows with several quality of service types, and installing support for flows with several types is RSVP's basic purpose.

There are two ways to map reservations onto circuits. Either each reservation gets its own circuits, so that each circuit carries the data of a single reservation, or several reservations are combined onto an aggregate circuit. In the first case the benefit is ease of implementation, and the cost is increased circuit setup time and the consumption of a greater number of circuits and resources. A multicast reservation request may translate into the setup of several circuits, while a unicast request always translates into a single circuit.

The aggregation model would allow large circuits to be set up between IP routers and hosts, managed much as point-to-point links are managed today, with traffic from several sources over several RSVP sessions multiplexed on the same circuit. It has a number of advantages: there is typically no signalling latency, since the circuits exist before the traffic starts flowing; the heterogeneity problem is reduced to a solved problem; and the dynamic quality of service problem is likewise reduced to a solved problem. It can be used with both point-to-point and point-to-multipoint circuits. Its problem is that the choice of what quality of service to use for a circuit is difficult without knowing the likely reservation types and sizes, though it is made easier when the circuits can be changed as needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Each reservation needs a wire with the right quality, and there are two philosophies. Give every reservation its own wire, which is simple but uses a lot of wires and takes time to set up. Or share a wire between reservations, which is efficient but means guessing the right quality for the wire in advance and gives up the freedom to renegotiate.

sections.title: When Receivers Ask for Different Things
sections.content:
Multicast heterogeneity occurs when receivers request different qualities of service within a single session, so the amount of resource requested differs on a per next hop basis. A related kind of heterogeneity comes from best effort receivers. In any IP multicast group some receivers may request quality of service and some may not. On a shared medium such as Ethernet, receivers that have not asked for resources can typically be given identical service to those that have, without complication. This is not the case with ATM, where any additional end-point of a circuit must be explicitly added, with costs attached and possibly without adequate resources. An RSVP over ATM solution therefore has to support heterogeneous receivers even though ATM does not provide that support directly.

Four mapping approaches are described. The full heterogeneity model provides a separate circuit for each distinct quality of service in a multicast session, including best effort and one or more qualities of service. It gives users exactly what they ask for but needs more network resources, and the amount of bandwidth used for duplicate traffic depends on the topology and group membership. The limited heterogeneity model limits the receivers of a session to either best effort or a single alternate quality of service, chosen either by higher level protocols or by dynamic renegotiation. Each edge device participating in a session then needs at most two circuits: a point-to-multipoint best effort circuit serving all the best effort destinations, and a point-to-multipoint circuit with quality of service serving the destinations that have a reservation. As with full heterogeneity, each packet must be duplicated at the network layer with one copy sent into each of the two circuits, and if any of the existing quality of service end-points cannot be upgraded, the new reservation fails even though the resources exist for the new receiver.

The homogeneous model has all receivers of a session use a single quality of service circuit, best effort receivers included, sized to provide the maximum resources requested by all the next hops. This matches the way the current RSVP specification handles heterogeneous requests and would be the simplest method to implement, but it has two specific problems: a user making a small or no reservation would share quality of service circuit resources without making, and perhaps paying for, a reservation; and a receiver may receive no data at all, because there are not enough resources to add it, in which case it is not added to the circuit and does not even receive best effort traffic. Not sending data to best effort receivers because of another receiver's request is clearly unacceptable, so the model can be extended with special handling for the case where a best effort receiver cannot be added to the quality of service circuit: a best effort circuit is then established for the receivers that could not be added, and only in that error case are senders required to replicate data. This is the modified homogeneous model. The last scheme is the aggregation model, already described, in which several reservations share one circuit.
sections.plainLanguage: In a multicast session some people want the good service and some do not. IP lets anyone join and take whatever is going. ATM cannot: every receiver has to be added to a circuit by name, and there may not be room. The memo lists four ways to cope, from one circuit per quality of service, through two circuits, to a single shared one sized for the greediest receiver.

sections.title: Control Messages, Encapsulation and Security
sections.content:
The RSVP messages themselves need a path. There are two main types, PATH and RESV. PATH messages are sent to unicast or multicast addresses while RESV messages are sent only to unicast addresses, and other RSVP messages are handled similarly, though this may be more complicated for RERR messages. So the circuits used for RSVP signalling must provide both unicast and multicast functionality, and there are four approaches to assigning them: use the same circuit as the data, a single circuit per session, a single point-to-multipoint circuit multiplexed among sessions, or multiple point-to-point circuits multiplexed among sessions.

Using the same circuit as the data needs no extra circuits and avoids ATM signalling latency for PATH messages, but there is a major problem when data traffic on a circuit is nonconforming: RSVP messages may be dropped. RSVP tolerates a moderate level of dropped messages, but excessive drops lead to repeatedly tearing down and re-establishing quality of service circuits, which is a very undesirable behaviour for ATM. A variation is to use the best effort data path for signalling, which avoids the nonconforming traffic problem but runs into congestion. Giving a single circuit per reservation doubles the number of circuits and adds latency, but is quite simple, and the signalling messages get their own traffic contract. Multiplexing point-to-multipoint circuits saves circuits but has problems when the destinations change, and multiplexing point-to-point circuits is flexible and can save substantially on signalling cost, since a point-to-point circuit can set up a reverse channel at the same time; in the core of a network the number of such circuits is approximately n(n-1)/2 where n is the number of IP nodes.

What quality of service to give the signalling circuits depends on the multiplexing and on the reliability of best effort circuits. Since RSVP signalling is infrequent, typically every 30 seconds, only a relatively small quality of service should be needed, which matters because a larger one risks the circuit setup being rejected for lack of resources.

Encapsulation has to be defined for both the RSVP packets and the IP data they control. The methods for transmitting IP over ATM, that is Classical IP over ATM, LANE and MPOA, are all based on the encapsulations in RFC 1483, which specifies two: LLC encapsulation, which allows multiple protocols over the same circuit, and VC-based multiplexing, which requires different circuits for different protocols. For RSVP over ATM any encapsulation can be used as long as the circuits are managed in accordance with the methods in the memo, though running several protocol data streams over one circuit with LLC encapsulation can cause the same problems as running several flows over one circuit. On security, the memo says the same considerations stated for RSVP and for ATM signalling support for IP over ATM apply, and that no additional security issues are raised.
sections.plainLanguage: The messages that ask for the good service need a path of their own, and there are four ways to give them one, from sharing the data circuit to a dedicated circuit for each reservation. Which one you pick trades circuit count against the risk of the setup messages being thrown away when the data path is busy.

viz.caption: THE FOUR WAYS OF HANDLING RECEIVERS THAT ASK FOR DIFFERENT SERVICE

cells: One circuit for each distinct quality of service, including best effort
Everyone gets exactly what they asked for, at the cost of more network resources
At most two: one best effort and one with quality of service
Each packet is duplicated, and a new reservation fails if an existing end-point cannot be upgraded
A single circuit sized to the largest request
Simplest to implement, but best effort receivers may share reserved resources or get no data at all
A single circuit, plus a best effort circuit in the error case
Best effort receivers always get data, and data is replicated only when a receiver cannot be added

viz.caption: TWO WAYS TO MAP RESERVATIONS ONTO CIRCUITS

cells: More circuits, more setup time and more resources consumed
Ease of implementation; each circuit carries a single reservation
Choosing the quality of service for a circuit is hard without knowing the traffic in advance
No signalling latency, and the heterogeneity and quality-of-service-change problems become simpler

viz.caption: THE FOUR WAYS TO GIVE THE RSVP MESSAGES A PATH

items.title: Same circuit as the data
items.text: No extra circuits and no signalling latency, but nonconforming data can throw the RSVP messages away.

items.title: One circuit per session
items.text: Twice the circuits and some extra latency, but the messages get their own traffic contract.

items.title: One point-to-multipoint circuit
items.text: Multiplexes sessions sharing an ingress router and egress routers, which complicates changing destinations.

items.title: Several point-to-point circuits
items.text: Flexible and cheap to signal, since each circuit can set up a reverse channel at the same time.
